title: When would you deliberately choose NOT to use Kafka?
shortTitle: When would you deliberately choose NOT to use Kafka?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log optimized for high-throughput streaming, replayable event history, and many consumers. You deliberately avoid it when its strengths do not match the problem: for simple request-reply where a synchronous call is clearer, for low-volume workloads where a managed queue is cheaper and simpler to operate, for strict priority or per-message scheduling and complex routing that a traditional broker handles natively, for tiny teams without the operational capacity to run a stateful cluster, and for workloads needing transactional joins across business tables where a database is the right tool.
s1_definition.analogy: Kafka is like building a dedicated high-speed conveyor system through National Bank of India that keeps a permanent record of every item and lets many departments read it at their own pace. That is fantastic for a flood of transactions feeding many systems. But if a teller just needs a yes-or-no answer from the credit desk right now, you do not build a conveyor, you make a phone call. And if the mailroom only handles a few letters a day, buying and maintaining an industrial conveyor is wasteful.
s1_definition.oneliner: Skip Kafka for simple request-reply, for low-volume or tiny-team workloads where a managed queue is cheaper, for priority or complex routing that a classic broker does natively, and when a database transaction is actually the right tool.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log optimized for high-throughput streaming, replayable event history, and many consumers. You deliberately avoid it when its strengths do not match the problem: for simple request-reply where a synchronous call is clearer, for low-volume workloads where a managed queue is cheaper and simpler to operate, for strict priority or per-message scheduling and complex routing that a traditional broker handles natively, for tiny teams without the operational capacity to run a stateful cluster, and for workloads needing transactional joins across business tables where a database is the right tool.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Kafka is like building a dedicated high-speed conveyor system through National Bank of India that keeps a permanent record of every item and lets many departments read it at their own pace. That is fantastic for a flood of transactions feeding many systems. But if a teller just needs a yes-or-no answer from the credit desk right now, you do not build a conveyor, you make a phone call. And if the mailroom only handles a few letters a day, buying and maintaining an industrial conveyor is wasteful.

**One line to remember:** Skip Kafka for simple request-reply, for low-volume or tiny-team workloads where a managed queue is cheaper, for priority or complex routing that a classic broker does natively, and when a database transaction is actually the right tool.

sections.s2_technical:
The first case is synchronous request-reply. If a caller needs an immediate answer, such as a fraud check that must return approve or decline before a transaction proceeds, a direct REST or gRPC call is simpler and clearer than publishing a request and correlating a reply through Kafka. You can do request-reply over Kafka, but it adds correlation ids, reply topics, and latency for no benefit when a simple call suffices.

The second case is low volume. Kafka is a stateful distributed system with brokers, replication, and now the KRaft controller quorum to operate, patch, and monitor. If you move a few hundred or a few thousand messages a day, the operational cost dwarfs the benefit, and a managed queue such as Amazon SQS or a lightweight broker gives you the same decoupling with almost no operations. Choosing Kafka here is over-engineering.

The third case is rich messaging features that traditional brokers provide natively. If you need per-message priority, where urgent messages jump ahead, or complex routing by headers and patterns, or per-message time-to-live and delayed delivery, RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ handle these out of the box. Kafka has no native priority queue and no native per-message TTL; you would simulate them with multiple topics and custom logic, which is awkward.

The fourth case is small teams and limited operational maturity. Running Kafka well means understanding partitions, replication, in-sync replicas, consumer groups, rebalancing, retention, and monitoring lag. A small team without that capacity is better served by a fully managed queue or even a database-backed job table, because an poorly operated Kafka cluster causes more incidents than it prevents. If you do need Kafka's model, a fully managed Kafka service removes most of the operational burden and changes this calculus.

The fifth case is when the real need is transactional data operations, not streaming. If you need to atomically update several business tables, run ad-hoc queries, enforce foreign keys, or join across entities, that is a database job. Kafka is a log, not a query engine, so forcing relational, transactional work through it is the wrong tool.

A senior nuance is that these are not absolutes. Kafka shines for high-throughput ingestion, event sourcing, replayable history, stream processing, and fan-out to many independent consumers, so the decision is about matching the tool to the access pattern. Another nuance is cost and latency: Kafka adds an asynchronous hop and at-least-once semantics that force you to design for idempotency and out-of-order delivery, which is unnecessary complexity when the interaction is naturally synchronous and exactly one caller cares about the result.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India has several integration needs, and an architect must decide which belong on Kafka and which do not. Blindly putting everything on Kafka would add cost and complexity where a simpler tool fits better.

Problem 1 — a point-of-sale terminal needs an instant approve or decline for Rajesh's card swipe. This is synchronous request-reply, so a direct call is right, not Kafka.

Problem 2 — the branch sends a handful of end-of-day summary emails. This is low volume, so a managed queue or even a scheduled job is right, not a Kafka cluster.

Problem 3 — a VIP customer's urgent wire must jump ahead of ordinary transfers. This needs message priority, which a classic broker does natively and Kafka does not.

Problem 4 — the transaction firehose feeds analytics, fraud, and ledger consumers that read independently and sometimes replay history. This is exactly where Kafka fits.

The code will implement a small decision helper that, given a workload's characteristics, recommends Kafka or an alternative and explains why, logging the recommendation for each banking workload.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four banking workloads with their characteristics.

Step 1 — the card authorization for Rajesh's swipe is marked as needing a synchronous reply, so the advisor immediately recommends REST or gRPC, because the terminal must get approve or decline right now and Kafka would only add latency and correlation complexity.

Step 2 — the end-of-day summary emails run at two messages per second with no replay and no fan-out, so the advisor recommends a managed queue, because standing up and operating a Kafka cluster for a trickle of emails is wasteful.

Step 3 — the VIP urgent wire needs priority so it can jump ahead of ordinary transfers, so the advisor recommends RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ, because Kafka has no native priority queue.

Step 4 — the transaction firehose runs at twenty thousand messages per second, feeds many independent consumers, and needs replay, so the advisor recommends Kafka, which is exactly what it is built for.

```
2026-10-24 22:30:01 [INFO] Card authorization (Rajesh swipe) → NOT Kafka — use REST/gRPC (caller needs an immediate reply)
2026-10-24 22:30:01 [INFO] End-of-day summary emails → NOT Kafka — use a managed queue (SQS) (low volume, simple decoupling)
2026-10-24 22:30:01 [INFO] VIP urgent wire transfer → NOT Kafka — use RabbitMQ/ActiveMQ (native message priority)
2026-10-24 22:30:01 [INFO] Transaction firehose (analytics+fraud+ledger) → USE Kafka (high throughput / replay / many independent consumers)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka is a distributed commit log optimized for high throughput, replayable history, stream processing, and fanning out to many independent consumers. I choose not to use it when the problem does not match those strengths. The clearest case is synchronous request-reply. If a caller needs an immediate answer, like a fraud check that must approve or decline a card swipe before it proceeds, a direct REST or gRPC call is simpler and faster than publishing a request and correlating a reply through Kafka.

The second case is low volume. Kafka is a stateful distributed system that you have to operate, patch, and monitor, so for a trickle of messages a day a managed queue gives the same decoupling with almost no operations, and choosing Kafka there is over-engineering. The third case is rich messaging features that traditional brokers provide natively, like per-message priority, complex routing, or per-message time-to-live. Kafka has no native priority queue, so if a VIP wire must jump ahead of ordinary transfers, RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ is the better fit.

The fourth case is a small team without the operational maturity to run a cluster well, because a poorly operated Kafka causes more incidents than it prevents, though a fully managed Kafka service changes that calculus. And the fifth case is when the real need is transactional, relational work across business tables, which is a database job, not a log.

In my National Bank of India work, I made exactly these calls. The card authorization path was synchronous REST because the terminal needed an instant decision. The handful of end-of-day emails went on a managed queue. A priority-sensitive wire path used a classic broker. And the transaction firehose, which ran at tens of thousands of messages a second and fed analytics, fraud, and the ledger with replay, was the workload that genuinely belonged on Kafka. Matching the tool to the access pattern kept the architecture simple and cheap where it could be and powerful where it needed to be.
